description: Spacxy is a team of Jain University computer science students working on AI, software and DevOps. For the Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we’re building a tool that lets users pick NASA Earth science variables and a region, plot how they change over time, and test whether the trend is statistically significant (rate of change, Mann-Kendall, t-test). We want to turn students and the public into data detectives who can see what is changing, where, and by how much.
summary:
Gaia Insights is a web application for exploring historical Earth-science observations. Users pick a variable and a region, study how it has changed since 1990, test whether the changes are statistically significant, and export a report.

It has a homepage and five guided pages: Data Explorer, Geographic Explorer, Trend Analysis, Change Detection, and Significance & Reports. Choices carry from page to page, and changing an earlier choice invalidates the results that depend on it.

Its main rule is scientific honesty. Every result must come from real data, with its product version, units, date range, region and method recorded. Missing data is never shown as zero, and spatial significance maps use false-discovery-rate correction.

The build is a React frontend in your "Velvet Fade" design, with a FastAPI backend using Xarray, GeoPandas and SciPy. The homepage hero may use the React Bits Pro globe as a decorative visual.

Current status: the pages and pipeline exist, and GPCP precipitation is the one fully real dataset. The temperature, humidity and soil-moisture variables were found to run on cropped test files and are now marked Unavailable. Real downloads for those, and for sea surface temperature, are the next step and need your NASA Earthdata token. The project was renamed from Earth Science Explorer, and the rename prompt is ready to run.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Gaia Insights is a web app for studying how the Earth has changed. A user is guided through five pages: choose a variable and dataset version, choose a country or draw a region on the map, see the trend over time, map where values rose or fell between two periods, and test whether the change is statistically significant. At the end they export a report. Behind the pages, a Python backend reads real NASA and NOAA data files, masks them to the chosen region, weights each grid cell by its area, and runs the statistics. Every result carries the dataset version, units, region and method that produced it. Precipitation (GPCP, 1990 to 2026) is fully working end to end.

What are the benefits?
Climate and environmental data is spread across providers, versions, grids and date ranges, so even a simple question takes expert time. Gaia Insights puts the whole workflow in one place and shows coverage, gaps and limits at each step, so a student, journalist or planner can get a trustworthy answer without writing code.

What is the intended impact?
To make evidence about a changing planet easier to explore and check. Every number can be traced back to a real data file, and the app says “Unavailable” rather than showing something it can’t support. That builds trust and teaches good scientific habits.

Tools and technology

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Recharts, Leaflet.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, statsmodels, GeoPandas, Rasterio, ReportLab.
  • Storage and operations: PostgreSQL with PostGIS, SQLAlchemy and Alembic, Docker, GitHub Actions, pytest.
  • Data: GPCP precipitation, NOAA OISST, NASA MERRA-2 and GLDAS, with Natural Earth boundaries.
  • Development: Antigravity AI agents. No special hardware was needed beyond an ordinary computer.

How is it creative?
It treats honesty as a feature. The app refuses to show made-up numbers, keeps missing data separate from zero, and flags a stale result when an earlier choice changes. Statistics are explained in plain language beside the results. The five-step journey and the editorial visual design make a heavy scientific tool feel approachable.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: dataset versions are never mixed, rates are converted to monthly totals, regional means are area-weighted, and multiple testing is corrected with false-discovery-rate control.
  • Data limits: some datasets cover only land or only ocean, and some start later than 1990.
  • Accessibility and responsiveness: colour is never the only signal, and layouts work on small screens.
  • Security and licensing: secrets stay out of the code, and data sources are credited.
  • Scope: with limited time, we chose fewer fully real data paths over many decorative screens.
